title: Runtime routing policy compiler for canary segmentation and SLA-aware failover
creator: Marco Chen
description: Background: We currently express deployment routing as a combination of simple traffic-splits + hard-coded fallbacks in multiple services (router, autoscaler, region-proxy). This has led to duplicate logic, slow rollouts when adding new variants, and inconsistent failover semantics across Dedicated/Hosted/Private planes. Problem: No single canonical artifact describes variant compatibility, per-region capacity tiers, and SLA-aware fallback order; runtime services re-implement heuristics (recent incident: ENG-34107) which caused a mis-ordered failover and a latency spike for an enterprise customer. Goal: Build a lightweight policy compiler that converts high-level deployment policies into a compact runtime routing DAG and a small set of runtime predicates. The output should support: deterministic canary segmentation, probabilistic A/B splits, shadowing, per-request SLA/cost scoring, region-aware failover edges, and auto-rollback triggers based on quality/regression signals. The compiler should also emit validation artifacts (compatibility matrix, human-readable plan) for the Console and CDS (deployment control system).
proposal: Design: Introduce a 'Routing Policy DSL' (text-first, JSON-backed) that encodes: 1) variant compatibility constraints (min_context_len, kv_cache_compat, quantized_compat), 2) routing priorities and tier scores (region, capacity_tier, cost_score), 3) canary segmentation rules (header-based, cookie, sampled-percent), and 4) rollback predicates (latency percentile, error-rate delta, quality-regression > threshold). The compiler will: - Validate variant compatibility with model metadata (model manifest) and produce a matrix of allowed edges. - Build a directed acyclic graph where nodes are candidate variant+region pairs and edges represent preferred fallback. - Annotate nodes with runtime scoring functions (SLO_score = f(latency, cost, tier)) that the runtime can evaluate cheaply. - Emit: 1) runtime DAG (compact binary JSON), 2) human plan (for Console), 3) canary metrics spec for monitoring/rollout automation. Runtime semantics: at request time evaluate segment rules; pick primary node; if node unavailable or SLO_score falls below threshold, follow first healthy fallback edge. For A/B: the sampling decision binds to the request id for sticky behavior. Shadow traffic: compile an always-send list with rate limiter hooks.
tradeoffs: - Centralized policy compiler simplifies reasoning but adds a single source of truth and a new validator step during deploys. - Compiler-generated DAGs may need recompile when variants change frequently; mitigated via incremental compiles. - Scoring functions add computational cost per decision; we keep them intentionally cheap (fixed-weight linear) and allow runtime caching of node liveness/state. - Conservative defaults: prefer latency SLO over cost when customer_impact==high. This can increase unit cost for critical customers.
implementation_notes: Language: small Rust service in deployments-runtime repo (existing infra, small binary), outputs compact JSON blob consumed by router agents.
Model manifest enrichments: add 'compat_flags' (kv_cache_safe, quantized_variant_id, max_sequence_len) — PR: github.com/redwood-inference/models/compare/manifest-compat#PR-204
Validation: compile-time checks for circular fallbacks and unreachable nodes.
Incremental compile: store per-deployment compile cache keyed by variant set + region table to avoid full recompile on minor edits.
Backward compatibility: router agents will accept both compiled DAG and legacy traffic-split config; new deployments default to compiled policy.
API: expose compile endpoint + dry-run to Console for preview and human review.
Runtime hooks: liveness (region/capacity tier) polled every 3s; ephemeral health marked 'down' if consecutive failures >3.
testing_plan: Unit tests for DSL parser, compatibility matrix generator, and DAG acyclicity checks.
Property tests for routing determinism under identical segment seeds.
Integration: end-to-end deploy using a staging Dedicated pool with 3 regions; run synthetic workloads that exercise canary, A/B, and fallback paths.
Chaos: simulate region partial outage and verify routing DAG falls back to next healthy node within 200ms decision time.
QA: manual Console review and a smoke test checklist for customer-facing deployments.
Canary: roll the compiler to 10% of deployments first, monitor 'routing-errors' and 'fallback-count' metrics for 48h.
acceptance_criteria: Compiler service builds and publishes compiled policy blob for a deployment with <=200ms compile time for typical variant sets (<=6 variants).
Router agent can evaluate routing decision in <=2ms P50 and follow fallback edges reliably when the primary node is unhealthy.
Console shows human-friendly compatibility matrix and an approval flow (dry-run -> approve -> promote).
End-to-end canary + A/B flow exercised in staging with sticky sampling and shadowing verified by logs and metrics.
Auto-rollback triggers fire and perform a controlled rollback when quality-regression > 5% over baseline for 5m window (hooked to quality-monitoring service).
rollout_strategy: Phase 1: deploy compiler service to staging, generate policies for a small set of internal services (chat-api, embeddings), validate in staging.
Phase 2: roll to 10% hosted deployments + one Dedicated customer that opts in; monitor for 72h.
Phase 3: open to general deployments as default, but keep legacy traffic-split adapter for 30 days.

Rollback: if routing.fallback.count or routing.decision.errors spike > 3x baseline or auto_rollback.events trigger incorrectly, revert compiler to previous stable and convert in-flight policies back to legacy config.
Post-mortem: any high-impact rollout issues require a blameless post-mortem with action items and a follow-up release.
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: compiler bug could create incorrect fallback order -> mitigation: conservative validator that prohibits changing existing live edges without manual approval for high-impact deployments.
Risk: decision CPU overhead -> mitigation: keep scoring functions simple, enable caching at router, and benchmark upper bounds.
Risk: mismatch across control plane and runtime versions -> mitigation: runtime accepts both formats and logs deprecation warnings in Console.
Risk: complex DSL leads to operator errors -> mitigation: provide Console visual editor + dry-run + lints.
open_questions: What is the canonical threshold for preferring SLO over cost for enterprise customers? (product input required)
Should the compiler incorporate live capacity signals (available GPUS) at compile time or rely solely on tiered static capacity at decision time?
Do we allow user-defined scoring weights in the policy or only product-defined presets?
